entries.title: IEP Basecamp 2026
entries.subtitle: Practical learning, networking and the IEP Learning Awards
paragraphs: Compass was looking forward to attending IEP Basecamp 2026, a full day for IEP members from Capability Partner organisations. The programme has four seminar sessions, time to connect with colleagues, and the IEP Learning Awards in the afternoon.
Sessions cover AI and the future of employment support, participant-centred practice, employer engagement, and health and wellbeing, with coffee, lunch and end-of-day celebration drinks.

Headline sponsor CCC Powered by Asuria UK, bringing together Asuria UK, PeoplePlus UK, Standguide Ltd, The Better Health Generation, Earlybird and Transform and Achieve, is making Basecamp free to attend for eligible IEP members. Other sponsors are The Digital College, Elevate Employment Services, CogniSoft Ltd, Serco and NCFE.
Basecamp is invitation-only. To find out about becoming a Capability Partner, contact your Partnership Manager or email angela.ramage@iemployability.org.

entries.subtitle: The Art of the Possible: Connecting the Dots

paragraphs: British Chambers of Commerce has officially launched its Global Annual Conference 2026, taking place at the iconic QEII Centre in London and hosted by Sky News presenter Sophy Ridge.

Built around the theme Delivering Growth, the conference will bring together business leaders, policymakers and innovators from across the UK and around the world to explore how opportunity can be unlocked, the economy strengthened and businesses supported to thrive.

Confirmed speakers already include Rt Hon. Ed Davey, Leader of the Liberal Democrats; Zack Polanski AM, Green Party Leader; and Rt Hon. Mel Stride, Shadow Chancellor of the Exchequer. A Senior Cabinet Minister and a Senior Representative from Reform UK will also be announced soon.

entries.title: NEET Trends and Youth Labour Market Discussion
entries.subtitle: Hosted by the Work Foundation
paragraphs: On 26 February, the Work Foundation and an expert panel reviewed the latest ONS figures on young people not in education, employment or training (NEET), and discussed what this means for young people, local communities, the labour market and Government.

The UK has had a significant population of young people aged 16–24 who are NEET for over 20 years, but the challenge for policymakers has evolved. The number remains stubbornly close to one million — around one in eight young people aged 16–24 — following a large post-pandemic rise.
The discussion also considered the Government’s response, including an £820 million youth participation package and work to investigate root causes of youth unemployment.

Panel: Sharon Thompson FIoL (West Midlands Combined Authority), Susannah Hardyman MBE (Impetus - Backing the best), Shuab Gamote, Chris Smyth (Financial Times), and Ben Harrison (Work Foundation at Lancaster University).

entries.title: Youth Jobs Grant: the opportunity is real, the job has to last
paragraphs: The Youth Jobs Grant offers employers up to £3,000 for hiring an eligible 18 to 24-year-old who has been on Universal Credit and out of work for six months or more. The scheme is designed to support up to 60,000 job opportunities over three years, and it is open across Great Britain until October 2028.

Payment is staged, not paid up front: £1,800 after six weeks and £1,200 after 18 weeks, once employment and earnings are verified through HMRC. Roles must be genuine paid work of at least 25 hours a week, last at least four months, pay at least the applicable minimum wage, and not replace an existing worker.

For Compass Consult, the grant is a useful way to reduce the upfront cost and perceived risk of recruiting young people who have been out of work for longer. It is not a substitute for job quality. Employers, Jobcentres, employability providers, local government and specialist organisations need to use it to build sustained employment, skills and progression, not just job starts.

entries.title: 1,000 new youth workers, and the integration test that follows
paragraphs: The announcement of 1,000 new youth workers across England matters for anyone working in youth employment, employability and skills. The first workers are expected to be in place by spring 2027, with a focus on community support for young people most at risk of becoming NEET.

Youth employment cannot be addressed through employment services alone. The new workers are expected to sit alongside education, training, health and crime-prevention services, building trusted relationships and connecting young people to sport, arts, mentoring and wider youth provision.

The recruitment drive sits inside a wider package: a £450 million Youth Matters Fund for facilities and activities, 50 Young Futures Hubs, more than £500 million through the National Youth Strategy, and the £820 million Youth Guarantee for 18 to 24-year-olds. That sits next to expanded employment support, the Jobs Guarantee and employer-led routes into work.

The practical test is integration. Local partnerships, clear referral and transition pathways, earlier identification of NEET risk, meaningful employer engagement, and better use of local data all matter more than another set of separate initiatives. Youth Matters was informed by research with more than 14,000 young people. The next phase is not only how many youth workers are recruited, but how well the system around them works.

entries.title: Staying Close and support for care-experienced young people

It pointed to enduring relationships, suitable housing and integrated mental health support, and said the test will be implementation through partnerships between local authorities, housing providers, health services, employers and specialist voluntary organisations, alongside education, skills and employment.
The post included the Department for Education's Staying Close implementation guide for local authorities, November 2026. No exact LinkedIn publication time was shown.

entries.title: Connect to Work: devolution should not mean fragmentation
paragraphs: Jon Smith wrote about an Employment Related Services Association report by Henry Foulkes on provider experiences of commissioning the Connect to Work programme. The same commentary appears on the company feed, with no separate Compass text.
He notes £1.18 billion invested in employment support across England and Wales, significant variation in commissioning, and a central message that devolution should not mean fragmentation.

entries.title: From Jobcentre Plus to the Jobs and Careers Service
paragraphs: The company post points readers to a blog by chief executive Jon Smith on the new DWP Jobs and Careers Service, published by the Institute of Employability Professionals.
On Jon's profile, that item is a repost of an announcement written by Scott Parkin FIEP. Scott Parkin wrote the announcement. The blog it describes is Jon's. This is one story, not two.

entries.title: Reflections on the Education Secretary's CST Conference speech
paragraphs: The company page introduced reflections by chief executive Jon Smith on Education Secretary Lucy Powell's speech at the Confederation of School Trusts Conference 2026. He welcomed the emphasis on widening opportunities, strengthening vocational education, and building stronger connections between education, employers and local communities.

entries.title: UK unemployment falls, but is the jobs market really improving?
paragraphs: The company page introduced commentary by chief executive Jon Smith on the latest unemployment figures. He argues that a falling rate is welcome, but that fewer vacancies, cautious recruitment and the need for sustainable, good work mean the headline figure should not be the only test.

entries.title: Adult Skills Fund: from national contracts to local commissioning
paragraphs: Compass describes the move away from nationally procured Adult Skills Fund contracts towards locally commissioned provision as a significant moment for the adult skills system. It says local authorities may be better placed to align investment with labour-market intelligence and employer demand, but that devolution will only improve outcomes if it comes with commissioning capacity, provider engagement and strategic coordination.

entries.title: Paid employment opportunities for young people with disabilities and health conditions
paragraphs: Compass welcomes a focus on genuine, paid employment opportunities for young people with disabilities and health conditions, rather than relying only on traditional employability interventions. It argues that preparation, reasonable adjustments, specialist support, employer engagement and in-work support will decide whether a short opportunity becomes a pathway into lasting work.

entries.title: Test, learn and grow: making improvement standard practice

entries.title: Children in care spending: invest in prevention, not only crisis
paragraphs: Jon Smith commented on Local Government Association analysis that councils spent £9.5 billion supporting children in care in 2025/26, compared with £6.6 billion in 2022/23. He argued for earlier intervention and joined-up support, including housing, mental health, education, skills and employment, without treating employment as a substitute for that wider support.
